findings.text: Only some of the character-literal lines can fail. `'\''` (line 183) and `'\\'`, `'\n'`, `'\u{1F600}'`, `'é'`, `'😀'`, `'\x7F'` (line 185) give the same counts even if they are not recognised as characters. A missed `'` is skipped as code, the backslash skips the next character, and nothing after it opens a string or comment. Only `'"'` and the lifetime and label lines can actually fail. To make the escape and Unicode forms count, put something after them on the same line that would open a block comment or a string if the literal were misread (for example `'\'' /* x '` followed by a comment line).

The line `let c = #"raw \"# // a backslash escapes nothing here` does not test what its comment says. A single-line raw string ends at the line's end either way, so if `\"` were wrongly treated as an escape the line would still be code and the next line still a comment. The counts would not change, so the single-line `#"…"#` no-escape rule is untested.

`local u = 'a\'--' -- trailing` gives the same counts whether or not the backslash escapes. If it did not escape, the string would end at `\'` and `--' -- trailing` would become a line comment, but the line is already code. So the Lua quote-escape rule is not tested.

The test is named for byte strings that go on over lines, but every `b"…"`, `br"…"` and `br#"…"#` in it opens and closes on one line. Neither a multi-line byte string nor a multi-line `br#` raw string is tested.

Outside the goal's list. The lookbehind `(?<!\w)` rejects Rust's raw C strings `cr"…"` and `cr#"…"#` (stable since Rust 1.77). The `#` is then read as code and the `"` opens an ordinary string that honours escapes. So `cr"C:\"` treats `\"` as an escape and stays open, swallowing the following lines. Allowing an optional `c` (like the `b`) fixes it.

Outside the goal's list. `#"""` always opens a multi-line raw string that only `"""#` closes. Swift's lexer treats `#"""…"#` on one line as a single-line raw string (for example `#"""quoted"#`), so the implementation leaves it open and counts the following lines as string code.

blind.summary: The goal is met. I traced every goal case through `readLine` and `closeAt`: nesting depth carries from line to line, raw-string runs and escapes work, Swift's `\#` escapes work, and Lua's `=` runs work. Rust tells character literals from lifetimes and labels, and Swift's `#if` and `#selector` start nothing. Other languages behave as before: the new `closeAt` matches the old escape rule, and nesting and fences are only enabled for Rust, Swift and Lua. I worked out each new test's expected counts by hand and they are right; I did not run `npm run check`. No blocker or major defects. What is left is minor: several test lines would pass even if the code were wrong, plus two edge cases just outside the goal's list.
